passages.happening: Jesus leaves Galilee and goes south into Judea and the land on the far side of the Jordan River. Crowds gather and he teaches them. Some Pharisees come to test him with a question: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” Jesus asks what Moses commanded. They answer that Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and send his wife away. Jesus says Moses wrote that rule because of their hard hearts. Then he goes back further than Moses, to the beginning: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. “Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.” Later, in the house, the disciples ask him about it again. He tells them that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and a woman who does the same commits adultery too.
passages.hearers:
The land ‘beyond the Jordan’ was ruled by Herod Antipas, the same ruler who had killed John the Baptist for speaking against his marriage (6:17-18). The Jewish historian Josephus says that Herodias divorced her first husband while he was still alive in order to marry Antipas, and that this went against the laws of their people (Antiquities 18.136). So a question about divorce, asked in Herod's land, was a dangerous one. It may have been a trap.

The question was also a live argument among Jewish teachers. The law in Deuteronomy 24:1 lets a man divorce his wife if he finds ‘some indecency’ in her. What did that mean? The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, records the later memory of the debate (Gittin 9:10). The school of Shammai said a man could divorce only for something shameful, such as unfaithfulness. The school of Hillel said he could divorce even if she spoiled his dinner. A later teacher, Rabbi Akiva, said even if the man found another woman he liked better.

In Jewish law at that time, only the husband could end a marriage. He did it by writing and handing her a certificate. The Mishnah gives its key words: she is now free to marry any man (Gittin 9:3). The certificate protected the woman, because it proved she was free to marry again. In Roman law, by contrast, a wife could divorce her husband as easily as he could divorce her. That is likely why Mark, writing for readers in the Roman world, includes the woman who divorces her husband (verse 12).

Jesus was not alone in going back to creation. One of the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Damascus Document, also uses ‘male and female he created them’ to argue against a man taking a second wife in his lifetime.
passages.ot:
Jesus joins two verses from the first pages of the Bible. Genesis 1:27: “male and female He created them.” And Genesis 2:24: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.”

The rule the Pharisees quote is Deuteronomy 24:1-4. Read closely, it does not command divorce. It assumes divorce happens and puts limits on it. The prophet Malachi also speaks for God about men who “break faith with the wife of your youth” (Malachi 2:15).
passages.hard:
Does this mean divorce and remarriage are never allowed? Christians answer in different ways, and each answer is held by careful readers. The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live, though it allows separation and can declare that a true marriage never existed. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Most Protestant churches read Matthew's words ‘except for sexual immorality’ (Matthew 19:9) and Paul's words about a spouse who leaves (1 Corinthians 7:15) as showing that unfaithfulness and desertion can free the innocent partner to remarry. Many also count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant. Some scholars argue that Jesus allowed separation but not remarriage. These notes do not decide between them.

What all of them share is Jesus' main point. God meant marriage to last for life, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined. In his world, Jesus' words also protected wives, who could be sent away with almost no say. Verse 11 makes the husband who divorces his wife answerable for wronging her.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.
passages.asks: Jesus moves the question from ‘What am I allowed to do?’ to ‘What did God intend?’ Ask where you tend to look for the edge of the rules instead of the heart of the command. If divorce has touched your life, by your choice or not, remember that Jesus spoke these words to defend the one with no power. He is not against you.

passages.happening: People bring little children to Jesus so that he will lay his hands on them and bless them. The disciples scold the people who brought them. Jesus sees this and is angry. “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!” he says. The kingdom of God belongs to people like these. Anyone who does not receive the kingdom like a little child will never enter it. Then he takes the children in his arms, puts his hands on them, and blesses them.
passages.hearers:
Children in the ancient world were loved by their parents, but they had no rank. They could not earn, argue, or give anything back. Important men did not stop their work for them. The disciples are acting as most people would have expected: the teacher is busy with grown-up matters.

Mark's word for ‘little children’ is the same one he used for the child Jesus set among the disciples in the last chapter (9:36), and for the little girl Jesus raised (5:39-41). Luke, telling this same scene, calls them babies (Luke 18:15).

Mark says Jesus was ‘indignant’. It is a strong word. In the Gospels this word is used of Jesus only here. Others are indignant at him or at each other; Jesus is indignant for the children.

The point of ‘like a little child’ is not that children are sweet or innocent. A child receives. A child cannot pay for a gift or earn a place. That is how the kingdom comes to anyone.
passages.asks: Who are the ‘little children’ in your church or home, the people who seem to slow down the important work? Jesus was angry when they were kept away. Ask too whether you try to earn God's welcome, or whether you can simply receive it, the way a child is carried.

passages.t: The man who went away sad
passages.happening: As Jesus sets out, a man runs up, kneels, and asks, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus asks why he calls him good, since no one is good except God alone. Then he lists commandments the man already knows. The man says he has kept them all since he was young. Jesus looks at him and loves him. He tells him he lacks one thing: sell everything, give to the poor, and he will have treasure in heaven. Then come and follow. The man's face falls. He goes away grieving, because he had great wealth.
passages.hearers:
The man runs and kneels. He is eager and sincere. Matthew calls him young (Matthew 19:20) and Luke calls him a ruler (Luke 18:18).

His question has a strange shape. You do not ‘do’ something to inherit. An inheritance is given by someone else. Jesus' answer will show that eternal life is received, not earned.

Jesus lists the commandments about how we treat other people: murder, adultery, stealing, false witness, honoring parents. He adds ‘do not cheat others’, which is not one of the Ten Commandments. It may stand in for ‘do not covet’, or echo the law's warning not to hold back a poor worker's pay (Deuteronomy 24:14). Either way, it is a pointed word for a rich man.

Mark's word for his ‘great wealth’ can mean property, such as fields and land. Selling it all would have changed everything about his life.
passages.ot: The commandments Jesus names come from Exodus 20:12-16. Moses promised blessing to those who obeyed (Deuteronomy 28:1-2), and many people took wealth as a sign of God's favor. That is part of why this scene, and the next, shocked the disciples.
passages.hard:
‘Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone.’ Is Jesus saying he is not good, or not God? Readers take this in two main ways. Some think Jesus is pressing the man to think about what he has just said: if only God is good, and you call me good, what are you saying about me? Others think Jesus simply turns the man away from flattering a teacher and back to God. Either way, Jesus goes on to do what only God may do. He asks the man to give up everything to follow him.

Does Jesus ask every Christian to sell everything? The church has read this in two ways. Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian teacher in Egypt, wrote a whole sermon on this passage, titled Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? He argued that Jesus asks us to be free from the love of money, not always to give it all away. Others have taken the words literally. A young Egyptian named Antony heard Matthew's version of this story read in church, gave away his family's land, and later went to live in the desert, as Athanasius tells in his Life of Antony. Many Christians since have followed one path or the other.
passages.asks: Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him before he asked anything hard. The hard command came from love. Ask what the ‘one thing’ might be for you, the thing that holds the place Jesus should hold. It may not be money.

passages.t: A camel and the eye of a needle
passages.happening: Jesus looks around and tells his disciples how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God. They are amazed. He says it again: how hard it is to enter the kingdom. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter. Now they are even more shocked. “Who then can be saved?” Jesus answers that with people it is impossible, but not with God: all things are possible with God. Peter says, “Look, we have left everything and followed You.” Jesus promises that no one who leaves home or family or fields for him and the gospel will fail to receive a hundred times as much now, along with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come. Many who are first will be last, and the last first.
passages.hearers:
The disciples' shock is real. If anyone could make it, surely it was the rich. They could give to the poor, keep the feasts, and pay for sacrifices. Wealth looked like a sign of blessing.

The camel was the largest animal in the land. The eye of a needle was the smallest opening anyone knew. Jesus is describing something impossible. Jewish teachers used the same kind of picture. The Babylonian Talmud, written down several centuries later, speaks of an elephant going through the eye of a needle as something that cannot happen (Berakhot 55b).

You may hear that the ‘Eye of the Needle’ was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall that a camel could squeeze through on its knees. There is no ancient evidence for such a gate. The story appears only many centuries later, and it softens what Jesus said.

Jesus calls the disciples ‘children’ in verse 24. It is the only time he does so in Mark, just after he has blessed the children.
passages.hard:
Is it wrong to be rich? Jesus does not say that wealth is evil. He says it makes entering the kingdom hard, so hard that only God can do it. Wealth tempts a person to trust what they own instead of God. But the answer in verse 27 is for everyone, rich or poor: no one gets in by their own strength.

The promise of ‘a hundredfold’ (verse 30) has been used to promise money to those who give to a preacher. Mark's words do not allow that reading. The houses and brothers and mothers are the new family of believers, who share their homes and lives. And Jesus adds ‘along with persecutions’. No one selling a get-rich promise mentions that.
passages.asks: Ask what you trust to make you safe: savings, skill, reputation, being good. Jesus says none of it can carry you through the needle. Then hear the hope: ‘all things are possible with God.’ If you have given something up to follow Jesus, look around at his people. They are part of the hundredfold.

passages.happening: They are on the road going up to Jerusalem. Jesus walks ahead of them. The disciples are amazed, and those following are afraid. Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them, for the third time, what is going to happen. He will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles, who will mock him, spit on him, flog him, and kill him. After three days he will rise again.
passages.hearers:
People always spoke of going ‘up’ to Jerusalem. The city stands high in the hills. From Jericho, the last town on this road, the way climbs about a thousand metres (over 3,000 feet) in roughly 25 kilometres (15 miles), from far below sea level to the hills of Jerusalem. It was a hard walk.

The ‘Gentiles’ means non-Jews. Here it points to the Romans, who ruled Judea. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment.

This is the most detailed of Jesus' three warnings (8:31; 9:31). Each step he names will happen in Mark's last chapters: handed over (14:10), condemned (14:64), mocked and spat on (14:65; 15:19-20), flogged (15:15), killed (15:37).
passages.asks: Jesus walks ahead. He is not dragged to the cross; he leads the way to it, knowing all of it. The disciples follow, afraid. Ask where Jesus might be walking ahead of you into something hard, and whether you can follow him even while you are afraid.

passages.t: Not to be served, but to serve
passages.happening: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come to Jesus. They want him to do whatever they ask. What is it? To sit at his right and his left in his glory. Jesus says they do not know what they are asking. Can they drink the cup he will drink, or be baptized with the baptism he will undergo? “We can,” they say. Jesus tells them that they will, but the seats at his right and left are not his to give. When the other ten hear about it, they are angry with James and John. So Jesus calls them all together. The rulers of the nations lord it over people. It must not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
passages.hearers:
To sit at a king's right and left meant to hold the highest places of honor and power. James and John have just heard Jesus speak of his death, and they are already planning the throne room.

A ‘cup’ in the Old Testament was often a picture of what God pours out for someone, very often his judgment. To be ‘baptized’ in ordinary Greek could mean to be plunged under, swamped, overwhelmed. Jesus is speaking of his suffering and death.

The other ten are angry. Mark does not say they were angry because the request was wrong. They wanted the same seats.

A ‘ransom’ was the price paid to set someone free: a slave, a prisoner of war, or a person whose life was forfeit under the law (Exodus 21:30). Everyone in Mark's world knew what it meant to be bought out of slavery.
passages.ot:
The title Son of Man comes from Daniel 7. There one like a son of man is given a kingdom, and “the people of every nation and language should serve Him” (Daniel 7:14). Jesus turns the picture over. This Son of Man came to serve.

The prophets spoke of “the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17), and a psalm says “a cup is in the hand of the LORD” (Psalm 75:8). In Isaiah 53, God's servant suffers for others, and “He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). Many readers hear that chapter behind ‘a ransom for many’.
passages.hard:
What does it mean that Jesus' life was ‘a ransom for many’, and who was paid? Christians have answered in several ways. Some early Christian writers spoke of a ransom paid to the devil, who held people captive. Others rejected that idea. Many later teachers, including the Reformers, taught that Jesus' death meets the demands of God's justice, with God himself paying in the Son. Others stress that the cross is a victory that frees captives from sin and death. Many hold that ‘ransom’ is a picture of cost and freedom, not a deal with someone who must be named. Scholars also debate how directly the saying draws on Isaiah 53, since Isaiah does not use the word ransom.

All Christians agree on what Mark puts first. The one who could have been served chose to serve, and he gave his own life so that many would go free.
passages.asks: James and John wanted glory without the cup. Ask where you want the honor of following Jesus without the cost. Then ask a plainer question. Where could you serve this week in a way no one will notice or thank you for? That is greatness, Jesus says.

passages.happening: They come to Jericho. As Jesus leaves with his disciples and a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus is sitting by the road. He hears that it is Jesus of Nazareth and starts to shout, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Many tell him to be quiet. He shouts all the louder. Jesus stops and says, “Call him.” They tell him to take courage and get up. Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, jumps up, and comes to Jesus. Jesus asks, “What do you want Me to do for you?” He answers, “Rabboni,” which means ‘my teacher’, “let me see again.” Jesus tells him that his faith has healed him. At once he can see, and he follows Jesus along the road.
passages.hearers:
Jericho lay deep in the Jordan valley, a warm green oasis below sea level. It was the last stop on the pilgrim road before the climb to Jerusalem. Before Passover the road would have been busy with travellers going up to the feast. A blind man had few ways to live other than begging, and a busy road was the best place for it.

‘Son of David’ was a royal title. It meant the promised king from David's family, the Messiah. This is the first time anyone in Mark calls Jesus by it, just before he enters David's city.

A beggar's cloak was likely the most valuable thing he owned. It kept him warm at night and may have caught the coins people threw. The law said a poor man's cloak given as a pledge must be returned by sunset, because “his cloak is the only covering he has for his body” (Exodus 22:27). Bartimaeus throws it away.

Mark names him. Most people Jesus healed in Mark have no name.
passages.ot: Isaiah promised a day when “the eyes of the blind will be opened” (Isaiah 35:5). God promised David a son whose kingdom would last: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13).
passages.hard:
Jesus asks Bartimaeus exactly what he asked James and John a few verses earlier: “What do you want Me to do for you?” The two answers are the point. The disciples asked for glory. The blind beggar asked for sight. Mark wants readers to notice who really sees.

Bartimaeus's cry, ‘have mercy on me’, lives on in Christian prayer. ‘Lord, have mercy’ (in Greek, Kyrie eleison) is sung in many churches. The Eastern churches' Jesus Prayer, ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me’, grew in part from cries like his and the tax collector's prayer in Luke 18:13.
passages.asks: The crowd tried to silence him, and he called out louder. Ask what you would say if Jesus stopped and asked you, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ Then notice what Bartimaeus did with his sight. He did not go home. He followed Jesus on the road, and that road led to Jerusalem and the cross.
